catalog_quote: [Parker 2009, p.6] All syllables must contain an onset except word-initially. Primary stress in the default case falls on the penultimate syllable of the prosodic word, but more sonorous vowels also tend to attract stress. The segment /ð/ can occur equally well in syllables bearing primary stress, secondary stress, or no stress at all, so stress placement does not crucially affect the occurrence of this phoneme and thus is not marked in the phonetic transcriptions cited in this paper. [Boevé & Boevé 2005 OPD, p.7] Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length) General rules for stress: Stress may be preferred on the penultimate syllable. Stress and length in Arammba may be conditioned by vowel sonorance. The syllable with the most sonorant vowel attracts stress: Possible sonority hierarchy for Arammba vowels: Most sonorous [a] á [æ] é / [ɛ] e, [ʌ] a, [ɔ] o, [ø] ó / [y] ú, [u] u / [i] i / [ə̆] è, [ɜ̆] à Least sonorous. The more sonorant vowels tend to sound longer.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (17 pp., text, PDF metadata 'Copy of Parker-Arammba.doc', March 2009). extracted text of printed page 6 (sec. 2 'Data', paragraph after example set (3)) contains the quoted passage word for word: 'Primary stress in the default case falls on the penultimate syllable of the prosodic word, but more sonorous vowels also tend to attract stress. The segment /ð/ can occur equally well in syllables bearing primary stress, secondary stress, or no stress at all, so stress placement does not crucially affect the occurrence of this phoneme and thus is not marked in the phonetic transcriptions cited in this paper.' Also confirmed p.12 remark: 'It is not the case that the vowels in the strong allo…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Default primary stress on the penultimate syllable of the prosodic word; a syllable with a more sonorous vowel (the OPD's hierarchy: á, é > e, a, o, ó > ú, u > i > è, à) tends to attract stress away from the penult. The primary source (Boevé & Boevé 2005 OPD, p.7) states the same two-part rule in hedged form: 'Stress may be preferred on the penultimate syllable. Stress and length in Arammba may be conditioned by vowel sonorance. The syllable with the most sonorant vowel attracts stress', adding that the more sonorant vowels sound longer. Read as sonority-driven weight sensitivity with a penultimate default.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Parker 2009 p.6 mentions that syllables can bear 'primary stress, secondary stress, or no stress at all', so secondary stress exists, but no placement rule is given in either source.
new_statements.exceptions: Sonority override of the penultimate default (both sources); no lexical exceptions listed. Parker p.9 (ctx line 624): the vowels of the 'strong' masculine-prefix allomorphs are not always stressed, nor the weak vowels /ə/ and /ɜ/ always unstressed. The OPD's wording ('may be preferred', 'may be conditioned') is tentative and the document is a draft 'posted as is without peer review'.
new_statements.domain_note: Parker: domain is explicitly 'the prosodic word'. OPD: word level, general rule, no phrase-level discussion; no tone in the language according to the OPD suprasegmentals heading (tone listed but nothing stated). Neither source marks stress in its transcriptions or gives stressed examples.
new_statements.identity_note: Sources describe Arammba/Aramba [stk] as a whole (OPD data from Mukfideben/Serki and Kiriwà villages; Parker notes dialects differ in /ð/ realization but gives one stress rule). Glottocode aram1253 as targeted. The SIL archive record for the OPD (entry 31303) lists Steve Parker as author, but the document itself credits linguistic work to Alma & Marco Boevé with Parker as data checker; citation given as Boevé & Boevé 2005 following Parker 2009's own reference list.
